1:
Nobody agrees where to place the psalm. Adam Clarke reports the Syriac heading, that David composed it when Gad the prophet warned him not to stay in Masrob because Saul sought his life; he notes that some assign it to the persecution by Saul or the rebellion of Absalom, but follows Calmet in making it a complaint of the captives in Babylon, and takes the workers of iniquity for the Babylonians. Keil and Delitzsch report that even Hilary opened his exposition by declaring that the superscription contains no history, giving up the question at the outset; they add that the Midrash finds the psalm very applicable to Daniel, cast into the lions’ den by the satraps through a delicately woven plot, and grant the aptness — but only because the psalm has no specially defined features and cannot with certainty be fixed to either of David’s two great periods of suffering. Augustine of Hippo reads it of the Passion and of the martyrs, who could not have been strong unless they had beheld him that suffered first, and remarks that the devil is now bound, so that the Church, once smitten altogether, is tried through individuals instead. John Calvin declines the question and describes the contents: complaint and prayer, dwelling on the injustice, cruelty and deceitfulness of the enemies, with the eyes turned at the close to a joyful deliverance.

On the voice of the prayer John Gill says the word carries groaning and crying, the psalmist being eager to be heard, and John Calvin that the voice is heard in prayer proportionally to the earnestness felt, the request for protection proving the life was then in danger. C.H. Spurgeon allows that speaking aloud often helps devotion but insists that mental prayer has a voice with God, since Moses is not read to have spoken at the Red Sea and yet was asked why he cried; he notes how constantly David turns to prayer, making it his battleaxe under every pressure, inward or outward. Matthew Henry observes that David asks for his life because he knows it is designed to be serviceable to God and his generation, and that pleading the fear of an enemy is no disparagement to his courage. Charles Ellicott would render the word not prayer but cry, or complaint.

Charles Ellicott sharpens the next pair of terms as well: not secret counsel and insurrection but secret league and noisy gathering. John Gill notes that the word denotes both the place where the wicked meet to consult and the counsel taken there, and instances Saul and his courtiers against David and the Jews against Christ. Adam Clarke puts the two in sequence — they plotted his destruction and then formed insurrections to accomplish it — and defines the workers of iniquity as those who made sin their labour and daily employment, their occupation and trade. C.H. Spurgeon turns the whole into petition: let their secrets be met by thy secret providence and their counsels of malice by thy counsels of love. On the whetted tongue Adam Clarke keeps the soldier in view, the enemy meditating the most provoking and defamatory words as a soldier whets his sword, with the bitter words as deadly as poisoned arrows; John Gill speaks of an edge set on words to ruin the reputations of good men; and Charles Ellicott, referring the figure to a string of parallels, quotes Shakespeare on slander, whose edge is sharper than the sword.
4:
Who the perfect man is that they shoot at divides the entry. John Gill gives four answers at once: David himself, who was far from perfect before the righteous law but quite clear and innocent in the matter of Saul; the Messiah, of whom David was a type, who is holy, harmless and undefiled; the church and people of God, not perfect in themselves but perfect in Christ Jesus; and the sincerity and uprightness of grace in them, which is what wicked men level at. Adam Clarke keeps to the ambush: they lurk so as to take their aim the more surely and not miss the mark, and they shoot suddenly, when no fear is apprehended because none is seen. Charles Ellicott puts the weight on the shooters rather than the target — they fear not, being utterly unscrupulous and fearing neither God nor man.

On the encouraging of themselves John Gill reads the verb as strengthening another, namely Saul, by arguments that would induce him to go on persecuting, or else the conspirators hardening themselves as men do when sentence against an evil work is not speedily executed. Charles Ellicott makes it a matter of method: they strengthen an evil thing for themselves, that is, they take their measures carefully and are prepared to carry them out resolutely, and the next clause is better read as calculating how to lay snares privily, the conspirators going over every detail in secret. On the closing question he canvasses three senses — who will see the snares, which he thinks weak; who is likely to see us, put indirectly; or, on the analogy of the same expression elsewhere, who careth for them?

The sixth verse is where the two closest readers part. Charles Ellicott suspects the text: the versions and some manuscripts point to a corruption, and he would read that they have completed their subtle measures, literally the planned plan. Adam Clarke takes the received text as emphatic rather than damaged. The verb used three times in the sentence signifies to strip off the clothes, so that the sense is that they investigate iniquities and perfectly investigate an investigation, which his old Psalter renders most energetically as ransacking wickednesses and failing not in the ransacking; to ransack, he explains, is to search every corner and leave no cranny unexplored. He then works the Latin word two ways, either from stripping a man bare so that he may be exposed and the more easily wounded, or from the footstep, which makes it a metaphor from hunting the stag — the slot being diligently sought out to learn where the animal has gone and whether he is old or young — and he sends the reader again to the rules laid down in the standard treatise on hunting. John Wesley is content that they study diligently to find new ways of doing mischief, and are cunning to contrive, conceal and execute.
7:
The turn of the psalm is a reversal of weapons. C.H. Spurgeon puts it shortest: they shoot, and shall be shot, by a greater archer who never misses, and while they were bending their bows the Lord had his ready and let the shaft slip when they least looked for it. Matthew Henry notices how the punishment answers the sin, and weighs the two arsenals: their arrows are many but they are only bitter words, and words are wind, and the curse causeless shall not come, whereas God has one arrow that will be their death, his curse, which is never causeless. John Gill identifies the arrow with the four judgments — famine, pestilence, sword and wild beasts — which are compared to arrows because they move swiftly, come suddenly on men crying peace, and penetrate deep and stick fast. Adam Clarke looks for a fulfilment instead, and thinks that if the psalm belongs to David’s time this is prophetic of the death of Saul, whom the archers pressed and sorely wounded.

On the tongue falling upon its owners John Gill supplies the instances and, with them, two more readings of the psalm: Haman hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai, to whom some apply it; the accusers of Daniel cast into the den they had procured for him, to whom others apply it; and Babylon, drunk with the blood of the saints, given blood to drink. Adam Clarke says only that the plottings and curses formed against him come upon themselves. C.H. Spurgeon presses the second clause, that all who see them flee away: their former friends give them wide space lest they perish with them, for who cares to go near Herod when the worms are eating him, or to sit in the same chariot with Pharaoh when the waves roar round him? Those who crowded about a powerful persecutor and cringed at his feet are the first to desert him in the day of wrath. John Wesley gives the same reason in a line, the fear of being involved in their destruction.

What the onlookers learn, and what the righteous do, occupies the close. Adam Clarke observes that the enemies had endeavoured to hide their mischief and that God punishes them so that all shall see it and acknowledge the just judgment; he adds that Calmet took the passage for a prediction of the destruction of the Chaldeans, after which the Jewish people became highly respected among the surrounding nations, though he thinks it applies more generally. John Gill makes the fear of these verses a reverent and godly fear rather than a slavish one, by which men learn righteousness and give glory to God. Charles Ellicott corrects two renderings: the clause about wisely considering is rather that they understand his work, and the final verb, given as glory, may mean shine forth clear, that is, have their cause acknowledged just, which is how the Greek and Latin seem to have taken it in rendering it that they shall be praised. John Gill insists that the gladness of the righteous does not rest on the ruin of the wicked simply considered but on the glory of God’s justice displayed in it and on his mercy to themselves, and John Wesley that it is for the honour of God, which by this means is vindicated.
